title: Does the Early Bird Really Catch the Worm? Or Could the Night Owl Get There First?
dek: Early risers earning more is only a correlation — you can't tell whether the social structure favors early risers or whether early risers are simply different people; and chronotype is biological, not a choice of willpower.
why: Medium information density, but it delivers two judgment-changing points — that chronotype is biological rather than a matter of willpower, and that early risers earning more is only a correlation — plus one actionable method for tuning your light exposure.
who: Founders and managers confused about the relationship between sleep schedule and work efficiency, especially those who need to design a team's collaboration rhythm or who have long been in conflict with the nine-to-five.
skip: The listener-mail segment from 16:56 to 19:00 is low on information; skip straight to the email-signature discussion at 20:00.

points.h: Chronotype is biological, not a choice of willpower
points.body: Angela and Stephen discuss the concept of chronotype — whether a person naturally becomes alert in the morning or the evening. Angela calls herself a lark, often waking before the alarm goes off. Stephen stresses that the 2017 Nobel Prize in Medicine went to circadian rhythm research, which shows this is biological — even plants have biological clocks, because the Earth rotates on its axis, there is day and night, and organisms must predict and adapt to that rotation. So the answer to "why don't you just become a morning person" is that this trait is extremely hardwired.

points.h: Teenagers sleeping late has biological evidence, it isn't laziness
points.body: Angela cites a 2017 PLOS ONE paper that used 12 years of diary data from the American Time Use Survey and found that chronotype is near-normally distributed both overall and within every age group, with the mean shifting systematically with age: later through adolescence, peaking at its latest around age 19, then shifting earlier. In other words, teenagers' bodies tending toward late sleep has evidentiary support. The paper also found that before age 40 men generally have later chronotypes than women, and after 40 it reverses. This supports the recommendation to push back school start times.

points.h: Later school start times have measurable benefits
points.body: In 2017 the Seattle school district pushed middle and high school start times from 7:50 to 8:45, nearly an hour later. Researchers from the University of Washington and the Salk Institute used this to measure sleep-wake cycles and found students' median sleep duration increased by 34 minutes, with measurable benefits. Based on these studies, the RAND think tank estimated that delaying middle and high school start times alone would yield $8.6 billion in economic productivity gains. This shows sleep schedule isn't an individual problem but a system design problem.

points.h: Early risers earn more, but it's only a correlation
points.body: Danish economist Jens Banke published a 2012 paper, "Do Morning-type People Earn More Than Evening-type People? How Chronotypes Influence Income," whose analysis showed early risers earn significantly more than late sleepers, and that being a morning type especially benefits men. But Stephen stresses this is correlational data and can't be called causal. Being an early riser correlates not only with income but also with happiness, productivity and health. So you can't distinguish: whether early risers are simply more productive people to begin with (a spurious correlation), or whether the social structure favors early risers.

points.h: COVID was a forced experiment, and people generally pushed back their wake times
points.body: Stephen says one thing learned from COVID is that many people are able to and prefer to work in very different ways. Angela adds that a big silver lining of COVID was a forced experiment, and research showed people really did change their sleep patterns: when they didn't have to be in the office at 9 and had more flexibility, people generally shifted their wake times later, more like weekends than weekdays. This proves the rigid nine-to-five system isn't immutable — it's just that before 2020 nobody was forced to test it.

points.h: The email signature solves an empathy problem, not an efficiency problem
points.body: Stephen says he's an early riser and often sends work emails at 5 a.m.; he thinks email doesn't demand an instant reply, so it's fine. But some people who receive an early-morning email think, "He sent it at 5, I only woke up at 7, I have to reply right away." So Angela added a line at the end of every email: "my work hours may not be your work hours, reply if you want, when you want." She says it's a tribute to her late friend Seagal Barsade, a scientist who studied emotion and empathy; Barsade was a famous night owl who wrote in every email, "my work hours may not be your work hours, please don't feel obligated to reply outside normal working hours."

points.h: The most effective lever for shifting your schedule is controlling light
points.body: Angela learned from Stanford neuroscientist Andrew Huberman's podcast that you can adjust your natural circadian rhythm by controlling light. Huberman recommends getting daylight within 15 minutes of waking, especially important in the low-sunlight winter months. Angela moved her laptop from her basement office to an upstairs spot by a window. Huberman also recommends minimizing light later in the day, i.e. dimming the lights at home after dark. Angela says she's also more careful about not playing on her phone, and instead reads on an old black-and-white-only Kindle, which she finds helpful.

points.h: From early bird to night owl is the biological clock shifting with age
points.body: At 17, Angela wrote a college application essay titled "Confessions of a Teenage Owl," in which she called sleep a "needless waste of time," said she slept only four hours a night, and claimed she was "just as healthy and twice as happy for it." Stephen says anyone in medicine or science today would want to delete that sentence. Angela is now 52, says she tries to sleep more, and compares herself to "the wise owl is to the early morning lark" — she went from early bird to night owl. This confirms the paper's finding that chronotype shifts with age.
